questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(x-y)\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=4t\,i+(4-4t)\,j$ for $t\in [0,1]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=4t,\,y(t)=4-4t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4-4t)\,j \\  & =4\,i+(-4)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(x-y)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+(x-y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}((x+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(x-y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(4t+(4-4t))\cdot 4+(4t-(4-4t))\cdot (-4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}16t+16-16t-16t+16-16t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}32-32t\,\text{d}t \\  & =32{\int }_{0}^{1}1-t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\,dx+(x+y)\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=i+t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=1,\,y(t)=t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j \\  & =j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\,dx+(x+y)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+(x+y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(x+y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+t)\cdot 0+(1+t)\cdot 1\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}1+t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}x\,dx+{z}^{3}\,dy-{y}^{2}\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the line $r(t)=\sqrt{2}t\,i+2t\,j+2t\,k$ for $t\in [1,4]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\sqrt{2}t,\,y(t)=2t,\,z(t)=2t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,k \\  & =\sqrt{2}\,i+2\,j+2\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,dx+{z}^{3}\,dy-{y}^{2}\,dz & ={\int }_{1}^{4}x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+{z}^{3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt-{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+{z}^{3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{2}t\cdot (\sqrt{2})+8{t}^{3}\cdot (2)-4{t}^{2}\cdot (2)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}16{t}^{3}-8{t}^{2}+2t\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}y\,dx+x\,dy+{z}^{2}\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the helix $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+t\,k$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,z(t)=t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx+x\,dy+{z}^{2}\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+{z}^{2}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+{z}^{2}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+{t}^{2}\cdot 1\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{t}^{2}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+{t}^{2}\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the helix $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+t\,k$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ].$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,z(t)=t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+k.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }-y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+t\cdot 1\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }1+t\,dt \\  & =(t+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}){|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =2\pi +\frac{(2\pi )^{2}}{2} \\  & =2\pi (1+\pi )\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}(3x+y)\,dx+x\,dy,$ where $C$ is a portion of the parabola parametrized by $r(t)={t}^{2}\,i+(4t-1)\,j$ for $t\in [0,2].$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)={t}^{2},\,y(t)=4t-1.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t-1)\,j \\  & =2t\,i+4\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(3x+y)\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(3x+y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}((3x+y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(3{t}^{2}+4t-1)\cdot 2t+{t}^{2}\cdot 4\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}6{t}^{3}+8{t}^{2}-2t+4{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}6{t}^{3}+12{t}^{2}-2t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{3}{2}{t}^{4}+4{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =[\frac{3}{2}(2)^{4}+4(2)^{3}-{2}^{2}]-[0] \\  & =[24+32-4] \\  & =52\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Construct a definite integral that is equivalent to $\displaystyle \int\limits_C (x^2+y)\,\mathrm{d}x + x\,\mathrm{d}y,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t) = t\,\mathbf{i} + t^2\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t\in\left[0,1\right].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t) = t, \qquad
y(t) = t^2.
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j \\  & =i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+y)\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(({x}^{2}+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+{t}^{2})\cdot 1+t\cdot 2t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{t}^{2}+2{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Construct a definite integral that is equivalent to $\displaystyle \int\limits_C x^3\,\mathrm{d}x + z\,\mathrm{d}y + y\,\mathrm{d}z,$ where $C$ is a portion of the helix $\mathbf{r}(t)=2t\,\mathbf{i} + \cos t\,\mathbf{j} + \sin t\,\mathbf{k}$ for $t\in[0,\pi]?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t) =2t, \qquad 
y(t) = \cos t , \qquad 
z(t) = \sin t.
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =2\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{3}\,dx+z\,dy+y\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }({x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2t)^{3}\cdot (2)+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}+({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_C y\,\mathrm{d}x -x\,\mathrm{d}y ,$ where $C$ is a portion of the ellipse parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)=\cos t\,\mathbf{i} + 3\sin t\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t\in[0,\pi].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t) = \cos t, \qquad
y(t) = 3\sin t.
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx-x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }y\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt-x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(y\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-3{sin}^{2}⁡t-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,dt \\  & =-3{t|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-3\pi \end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Line integrals with respect to $x$ and $y$ often come in pairs. For example, 

$$
\int\limits_C (x+y) \, \textrm dx + \int\limits_C (x-y) \, \textrm dy.
$$

We usually express a sum of line integrals with respect to $x$ and $y$ as a single integral. In the case above, we can write this sum as

$$
\int\limits_C (x+y) \, \textrm dx + (x-y) \, \textrm dy.
$$

Let's evaluate this integral in this case where $C$ is given by the line segment

$$
\mathbf{r}(t)=\underbrace{(6t+1)}_{x(t)} \,\mathbf{i} + \underbrace{(2t+1)}_{y(t)} \,\mathbf{j}, \qquad t\in\left[0,1\right].
$$

Along the path $C,$ we have

$$
x = 6t+1, \qquad y = 2t+1.
$$

Computing the derivative of $\mathbf r(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+1)\,j \\  & =6\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the line integral by applying a change of variables, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,\text{d}x+(x-y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x+y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+(x-y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}((x+y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(x-y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(6t+1+2t+1)\cdot 6+(6t+1-(2t+1))\cdot 2\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(8t+2)\cdot 6+(4t)\cdot 2\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}48t+12+8t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}56t+12\,\text{d}t \\  & ={28{t}^{2}+12t|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =28+12 \\  & =40.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Line Integrals With Respect to X, Y, and Z
tutorials.problem:
Let $f(x,y,z)$ be a function of three variables and $C$ be a path in three-dimensional space. Suppose we want to calculate the following sum of line integrals:

$$
\int\limits_C f \, \textrm dx + \int\limits_C f \, \textrm dy +  \int\limits_C f \, \textrm dz
$$

For notational simplicity, we can express this as a single integral, as follows:  

$$
\int\limits_C f \, \textrm dx + f \, \textrm dy +   f \, \textrm dz
$$

As before, we can evaluate this integral by parameterizing the curve $C$ using the parameter $t\in [a,b]$ and then rewriting the integral using a change of variables, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f\,\text{d}x+f\,\text{d}y+f\,\text{d}z & ={\int }_{a}^{b}f\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+f\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+f\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(f\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+f\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+f\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we often omit the large parentheses and simply write

$$
\int_a^b f\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} + f \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t} +   f \dfrac{\textrm d z}{\textrm d t} \,\textrm d t.
$$

Finally, it can be helpful to switch to prime notation for the derivatives when dealing with complex integrands. In this case, the above formula becomes

$$
\int_a^b f x'+ f y' +   f z' \,\textrm d t,
$$

where the primes denote differentiation with respect to $t.$
tutorials.title: Line Integrals With Respect to X, Y, and Z
tutorials.content:
Let $f(x,y,z)$ be a function of three variables and $C$ be a path in three-dimensional space. Suppose we want to calculate the following sum of line integrals:

$$
\int\limits_C f \, \textrm dx + \int\limits_C f \, \textrm dy +  \int\limits_C f \, \textrm dz
$$

For notational simplicity, we can express this as a single integral, as follows:  

$$
\int\limits_C f \, \textrm dx + f \, \textrm dy +   f \, \textrm dz
$$

As before, we can evaluate this integral by parameterizing the curve $C$ using the parameter $t\in [a,b]$ and then rewriting the integral using a change of variables, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f\,\text{d}x+f\,\text{d}y+f\,\text{d}z & ={\int }_{a}^{b}f\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+f\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+f\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(f\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+f\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+f\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we often omit the large parentheses and simply write

$$
\int_a^b f\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} + f \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t} +   f \dfrac{\textrm d z}{\textrm d t} \,\textrm d t.
$$

Finally, it can be helpful to switch to prime notation for the derivatives when dealing with complex integrands. In this case, the above formula becomes

$$
\int_a^b f x'+ f y' +   f z' \,\textrm d t,
$$

where the primes denote differentiation with respect to $t.$
